Book and Problems Review

Research into your 22 feedback items on the NightHall book and LiteSpec 3.0.0. Eight Muse workers (four Muse Wonder, four Muse Spark) researched the repositories and the web; every claim used here was checked against the repository or the source page. 2 November 2026.

Summary and Decisions

Your feedback has three root causes, and each needs a different kind of fix. Some of it is about what LiteSpec records, some about how the book shows it, and some about what NightHall wrote.

17 of 30
NightHall problems that are not customer pains: market facts, legal duties, the founder's own risks
16 of 23
NightHall actors that "hold no role": systems and internal machinery, not actors
0 of 942
requirements the book can call met, because the model holds no test run
0 of 111
features marked shipped, although 1,281 of 1,286 use cases have code
  1. LiteSpec lets too much into Intent. The standard says product intent includes "how the company runs and what comes next" (docs/core/intent.md:28). The problem type has no rule about whose pain it is, and an actor may be a system. So NightHall's founder worries, market fact sheets, government address services and background jobs all sit beside the organizer's real pains. That's why you read "all kinds of problems and complaints".
  2. LiteSpec has no slot for what a reader needs. A journey has no description. A problem has no field for who exactly, what it costs them, or how strong the evidence is. A term like "design partner" can be used 130 times without a definition. Risk is a number (tier 1 or 3) that names nothing. LiteSpec models what the machine needs carefully and what the reader needs barely at all.
  3. The book answers the wrong question first. Every page leads with approval (Status, Reason, Owner, Risk Tier). It hides the record type, never prints the id, and moves "who" and "what it connects to" into the right rail. The only completion signal it could compute collapses to "not met" because no test run is loaded.

What I recommend, in one table

#RecommendationWhereSection

2Give every problem a named primary sufferer with a segment line, a cost today, a workaround today, and evidence entries whose strength is computed. Approval requires reported or observed evidence.LiteSpec3
3Allow only people and organizations as actors. Each external system stands alone, and internal machinery is never an actor.LiteSpec4
4Add a required description to journeys: who walks, what starts it, what good looks like, why it matters.LiteSpec5

8Use one page anatomy for every record type: type and its question visible, id with copy controls, place in the tree, one aligned field table, prose, links grouped by relation, then completion. No badges for facts and no cards inside cards.Book10, 11

Items 1, 3, 4, 5 and 11 break the current LiteSpec release. That's allowed: LiteSpec keeps no compatibility work between releases. Five decisions are yours to make; they're listed under Decisions for you.

The Book Today

These are the pages you open. The numbered notes mark what a reader landing on one cold can't find.

1What a Problem Is

"It should be clear what problems should be about. In NightHall I'm reading all kinds of problems and complaints." "Better categorization of problems." "It should be clear WHO we think has the problem." "I'm not sure a problem like v1-does-not-fit-the-calendar should be in LiteSpec at all."

Background

LiteSpec defines a problem as "one pain or job someone has today" (glossary) and requires only two fields, statement and situation. The affects link to actors is optional. The intent page states the right test: write a problem "when you can describe it without a solution, with evidence". Nothing checks it.

What we found

A Wonder worker read all 30 NightHall problems and sorted them by what kind of claim the statement makes. I checked the counts.

Kind of claimRecordsExamplesBelongs in
Customer pain: someone outside NightHall suffers today, works around it, pays a cost13unwanted-tickets-strand-money, late-held-ticket-money, safety-answers-on-paper, organizers-doubt-a-new-supplierproblem
Market condition: true of a segment whether or not anyone suffers it this week4costly-small-markets, german-clubs-under-pressure, costs-rise-demand-turns-lateresearch, summarized on its topic
Legal duty: an authority can hold someone to it3duties-before-the-first-sale, law-before-the-first-invoiceconstraint
NightHall business or delivery risk6v1-does-not-fit-the-calendar, more-work-than-march, proof-before-commitment, support-cost-decides-the-businessroadmap decision, goal, risk row
Internal complaint about NightHall's own work or staffing3site-gaps-before-first-contact, trust-without-a-teamoutside LiteSpec, or a known gap
Why NightHall refuses features1refusals-protect-the-perimeterdecision

Three patterns show up again and again:

  • The affected actor is whoever is nearby, not who suffers. platform-staff ("the people working for NightHall itself") is the primary sufferer on 9 of 30 problems and is named on 13. A problem type whose sufferer is the supplier, in a third of its records, is a risk register under another name.
  • Near-duplicates hide behind different words. late-held-ticket-money and late-payouts-double-fees; support-cost-decides-the-business and support-cost-per-ticket; assembled-event-stack and scattered-event-tooling; a-saturday-night-at-risk, organizers-doubt-a-new-supplier and switching-on-reliability. Nothing forces a statement precise enough for the overlap to show.
  • "Approved" certifies a signature, not evidence. All 30 are approved, including records whose own evidence says "inferred, not measured" (every-stranger-waits.md) or "the author's own arithmetic, not a measurement" (more-work-than-march.md).

What practice says a problem is not

A Spark worker compared 13 methods: Opportunity Solution Tree (Teresa Torres), Jobs To Be Done (Ulwick and Christensen), job stories, Lean Canvas, Amazon's PR/FAQ, Shape Up, the d.school point of view, Nielsen Norman Group, the GOV.UK Service Manual, BABOK and ISO 29148, SVPG's four risks, and assumption mapping. Every method except Shape Up makes the sufferer a required part of the statement, and almost all keep these apart from the problem:

  • A solution in disguise. Nielsen Norman Group: a problem statement should "Not contain a solution. Leave solutions out of your problem statement." Its checklist is the five Ws: who is affected, what, where, when, why it matters. (Checked on nngroup.com.)
  • A risk, which is something that might happen. A problem is pain someone has today. Cagan's viability and feasibility risks belong to the business and the team, not the customer.
  • A goal. "Increase organizer retention" is a goal. "An organizer can't tell whether a new supplier will pay out on time" is a problem.
  • An internal constraint. Shape Up separates the user's problem from "our" appetite and team. Your calendar is a constraint on the plan, not a pain someone else suffers.

Where v1-does-not-fit-the-calendar belongs

Not in the problem type. Its sufferer is the founder, its pain is an estimate ("about 210 working days ... against five months"), and no feature solving it could be proved by running the application. It's a delivery risk, and its own text already points to topic/risks. Two workers reached this independently. Only one feature links to it (trust-first-build-order), and that link should go to the scope decision instead. Its sibling more-work-than-march is worse: 13 features cite it as the pain they "solve" by being deferred. That teaches every future agent that deferral solves a customer pain.

Recommendation

Add an admission rule to LiteSpec: a problem's primary sufferer is a person or organization outside the team building the product, and its situation is stated without schedule, effort or headcount. Check it: a problem whose affects names only staff actors fails. In NightHall, keep and deepen the 13 customer pains. Move the other 17 to the record types listed above; NightHall already has all of them (29 constraints, about 30 research records, 8 goals).

For grouping, don't add a hand-written category field. Group problems in the book by primary affected actor, then by the goal their solving features advance. Both are computed from links, so the grouping can't drift, and "who has it" becomes the first thing you see in the list.

The two workers differed on categories. One proposed a closed category list (organizer pain, buyer pain, adoption trust, operator pain); the other proposed computed grouping only. I chose computed grouping because those category values are NightHall words that LiteSpec can't own, and the admission rule does the real sorting.

2The Four Named Problems

"a-saturday-night-at-risk is written vaguely; it is not clear what the problem is. every-stranger-waits: vague, not enough context. Also more-work-than-march and proof-before-commitment."

Each is vague for a different reason. The rewrites below come from the problems audit, at the depth recommended in section 3. Where a record holds no fact, the rewrite names the gap as an open evidence item instead of inventing one.

A Saturday Night at Risk: a metaphor instead of a sufferer

Now

Statement: A new ticket supplier asks an organizer to risk a Saturday night, with money, the door, and buyer trust together.

Situation: Organizers compare proceeds safety, payout timing, conversion, on-sale stability, and offline scanning before they move. A pilot partner forgives a missing help article, but a stranger decides in ten minutes. The difference is trust pages with proof. Described on the launch page.

Evidence: a pointer to the viability research, with no claim, date or strength.

Rewrite

Title: Organizers Will Not Move a Night to an Unproven Supplier

Who: Organizer, specifically a recurring independent promoter in the Dutch pilot segment deciding whether to move a Saturday club night before the season.

Statement: Before an organizer moves a night to a supplier they have never run a door with, one bad night (money held, door stalled, buyers blaming the organizer) costs more than a season of fee savings, so they will not move on a promise.

Cost today: They stay with the incumbent and keep its fees and payout timing.

Workaround: Don't switch, or switch one small night and run the door in parallel.

Evidence: Tibbaa collapsed mid-season in August 2024, leaving venues unpaid (verified, market research). The five comparison criteria are judgement from the launch topic. Open: no interview yet prices one failed night.

What's wrong today: the grammatical subject is "a new ticket supplier", which is NightHall. There's no moment, no cost and no workaround. It also overlaps organizers-doubt-a-new-supplier, which names the same sufferer better. Merge it into that record unless you want the first-night decision kept as its own problem.

Every Stranger Waits: the wrong actor

Now

Affects: Visitor ("a person reading public pages without signing in")

Statement: Organizers want to see the door and the money before a call, and one founder cannot give every visitor a call.

Evidence admits: "That a four-minute tour converts strangers to conversations is inferred, not measured."

Rewrite

Title: Organizers Cannot Judge NightHall Without a Call

Who: Organizer, not yet a customer, comparing ticket sellers before any conversation.

Statement: An organizer comparing ticket sellers cannot see how NightHall handles the door and the money without booking a call, and most will not book the call.

Cost today: They default to the incumbent, and NightHall loses the comparison without learning it happened.

Evidence: About thirty services sell into the Netherlands and the largest publish no organizer price (verified, competitors research). Tour conversion is inferred. Open: no funnel counts exist yet.

The sufferer is a prospective organizer, and NightHall has no actor for that. The record borrowed visitor and inherited its shallowness. The statement also describes a missing feature (the demo), not a pain. Recommendation: name actor/organizer with a segment line "not yet a customer, comparing sellers". Don't create a "prospective organizer" actor, because a lifecycle stage isn't a kind of actor.

More Work Than March: arithmetic filed as a pain

Now

Affects: Platform Staff

Statement: Version 1 cannot hold everything, and one person cannot build it all by March.

Evidence: "The 210-day capacity figure is the author's own arithmetic, not a measurement."

Becomes a decision

Title: What Leaves Version 1, and What Brings It Back

Owner: the founder. Not a customer.

Context: The listed scope needs roughly 210 working days from one person against about five months to launch. The estimate is a day per small item and three per medium item, the author's arithmetic. Parked items carry triggers that bring them back on evidence.

Success: goal/m2-ten-live-events, not the absence of this record.

Delete the problem. The 13 features that cite it should cite the scope decision, or cite nothing, since deferring a feature solves no customer's pain.

Proof Before Commitment: a validation gate filed as a pain

Now

Statement: No organizer data is held yet, and the next evidence is signatures and advice, not more code or desk research.

A stranger can't tell whether buyers, organizers or NightHall want the proof.

Already exists as a goal

goal/m1-five-signed-partners: "Five design partners holding 100,000 tickets a year between them sign before the pilot", with a why-it-matters line and a due date. Fold the gates (processor allocation, Dutch legal and tax review) into the milestone decision, and delete the problem.

The statement describes a method ("the next evidence is signatures"), not something anyone suffers. The machinery already exists in better shape as the M1 goal and feature/milestone-gates.

3Problem Shape and Checks

"Problems should be more detailed, with much more explanation, thought and evidence behind them."

Longer prose alone won't help. NightHall's problems are already prose, and they came out as one compressed situation plus a pointer. The fix is fields for the parts a check can read, and fixed explanation sections for the parts only a person reads. NightHall's best record shows the depth is achievable: unwanted-tickets-strand-money names the sufferer (a buyer who can't attend), the size (8.2 percent of tickets resold, 87.6 percent at or below the original price, from a study of 3,175 residents) and the workaround (a stranger on Facebook).

Proposed fields

FieldRule
affectsRequired. The first entry is the primary sufferer: a person or organization actor, never a system and never only staff.
affectsSegmentOne line qualifying the primary sufferer: segment, size if known, geography. This tells you who without opening the actor page.
statementOne sentence: sufferer, condition, consequence. The product is never the subject, and no solution is named.
situationWhen it happens and what the person was trying to do. Never a bare pointer to another page.
costTodayWhat it costs them now in their own units (money, hours, a lost night), or unknown plus an open question naming the source that would price it.
workaroundTodayWhat they do instead, and why that fails.
evidenceA list of claim, source (research id or URL), readOn and kind: observed, reported or assumed. The book shows the strongest kind present, computed and never typed.

The explanation file uses fixed sections in this order: Who Has It (one concrete occasion), What They Do Today, Evidence, What Would Retire It.

Proposed checks

CheckCatchesLevel
Primary sufferer is a person or organization outside the teamFounder risks and system "sufferers"Blocking
Cost and workaround present, or unknown with an open questionSlogansBlocking
Approval needs at least one observed or reported evidence entry; assumed-only evidence stays draft"Approved" on admitted inference. This alone would have held 5 of the vague records at draft.Blocking
Statement names no product, feature or solution verbMissing features disguised as painsAdvisory (word list)
Two problems with the same primary sufferer citing the same topic must name each other or mergeThe four duplicate clustersAdvisory
Recommendation

Adopt the fields and the first three checks in LiteSpec. Then put every surviving NightHall problem back to draft until it meets the evidence rule. "Approved" on admitted inference is the defect that hides all the others in the book.

Evidence grading follows practice: observed (watched it happen), reported (a sufferer said it), assumed (nobody outside confirmed it). The GOV.UK Service Manual treats needs written from assumptions as not yet needs.

4Actors Such as Address Lookup

"Some actors don't make sense at all, e.g. Address Lookup."

Cause

LiteSpec makes this happen. An external system must name the actor it acts as (schemas/record.schema.json, required actor), and an actor's kind may be system. So each of NightHall's 12 outside systems got a same-named actor twin, whose summary restates the system and then says "it holds no role". Four more system actors are internal machinery: event-reaction, recurring-job, message-transport and presentation-renderer. They were promoted to Intent because journey steps needed an actor value at handoffs. Result: 7 people, 1 organization and 15 systems. 16 of 23 records say "holds no role", which concedes they aren't actors.

Practice

  • UML: an actor is a role, and it is external to the system. Internal handlers fail outright.
  • Cockburn use cases: a system can be a supporting actor only if it takes part in a use case toward a goal. A pure receiver (the mailbox, a wallet) is not one. DNS is nothing.
  • C4: people and software systems are different boxes at different levels. Infrastructure never sits beside people.
OptionProsCons
A. Actors are people and organizations only. External systems stand alone; machinery isn't an actor.The actor list becomes the people who use NightHall. It matches C4 and the plain meaning. Removes 16 records.Steps and links naming system actors need rewriting. Steps run by a reaction or job carry no actor.
B. Keep system actors only for systems that take part in a use caseSmaller change; keeps integrationThe line between participant and receiver gets argued forever, and twin records remain
C. Keep the records, split them in the book's displayNo record changesThe confusion stays in the model, and summaries are written twice
Recommendation

Option A. Change actor kind to person or organization, make the external system's actor link go away, and add a check that every actor is named by a journey, a problem or an access position. Keep organizer as an organization actor: it's the customer who has the problems. Model integration as an external system calling through API entry points.

5Journeys Without a Description

"Journeys have no description."

Correct, and it's by schema: a journey has actor, serves, finishedWhen, steps, betweenSteps and cites, but no summary. Every sibling type has one: product, actor and screen have summary, goal has whyItMatters, feature has offering. The prose a journey does have answers other questions. betweenSteps covers branch order, the Example section describes one occasion, and Before It Starts lists preconditions. None says who it's for, what starts it, or why it matters.

Practice agrees. Nielsen Norman Group's journey map starts with Actor and a Scenario with expectations. Jeff Patton's story map writes "who you are mapping for and what goal they are trying to achieve" at the top.

Recommendation

Add a required description field of up to four sentences (who walks, what starts it, what good looks like, why it matters), rendered first on the page. finishedWhen stays the checkable end state. Separately, split sell-tickets-for-an-event into the four journeys LiteSpec's own example already names.

journey/request-a-refund
description: |-
  A buyer who cannot attend asks for their money back from the order page they already hold.
  It starts when the buyer opens the order link and ends with money on the card they paid
  with, or a recorded refusal carrying the organizer's reason.
  Refunds are where buyer trust is won or lost after the sale, so this walk works without an
  account and without asking the buyer twice.

6Design Partners and Undefined Terms

"What the heck is Design Partners?"

"Design partner" appears about 130 times across NightHall's records and prose: goals, pricing, sales, launch, economics, lead kinds and offer codes. It is never defined. The glossary holds it only as a lead-source label (code: design-partner). Worse, term/partner is defined, and means something else: "Another business that sells the organizer's tickets to its own audience for a share the organizer sets", which is a sales channel.

From use: a design partner is one of the first ten organizers, signed by hand in Rotterdam and Amsterdam before the public launch, who shape the product through interviews and pilot nights in return for Flat rate at EUR 99 a month for 12 months. That matches the common SaaS meaning.

Recommendation

Now: write term/design-partner with that meaning, and add "not a design partner" to term/partner. In LiteSpec: the book links every glossary term in prose to its definition, and an advisory check flags a capitalized phrase used in three or more records that matches no term. Make the check blocking once its list of ordinary phrases settles.

The writing worker proposed renaming design partners to "reference organizers". I rejected that: the name is fine and common. What's missing is the definition.

7Risk Tier

"Risk tier sucks."

Today risk holds any of money, physical-access, personal-data and access. Any value makes a record tier 1, and no value makes it tier 3 (docs/core/model.md:390). It has three defects:

  1. Tiers 1 and 3 with no 2. It's a yes-or-no wearing numbers that promise a scale. Every reader asks where tier 2 is.
  2. The label says nothing. "Tier 1" hides what's at stake, even though the record already says "money". Data classification works the other way round: the level's name is the content (public, internal, confidential, restricted).
  3. It mixes a risk class with an approval rule. Tier 1 means both "touches money or data" and "a named person approves". In a one-owner project, the approval half disappears while the label stays. ITIL keeps the change type separate from the approving authority and maps one to the other in a table.
OptionProsCons
A. Show the risk class by name, with a project table mapping each class to its approvalThe label says what's at stake. Approval rules can differ per project without touching about 790 NightHall records. No phantom numbers.Every "tier 1/3" mention in the standard, checks and book changes
B. Rename to two honest levels (standard, elevated)Smallest changeStill merges class and approval, and still hides which risk
C. Impact times likelihood on every recordFinest grainAbout 790 subjective scores to write and defend: process for show
Recommendation

Option A. On a page this reads as an ordinary field: Risk: Personal data, approved by a named person. A record with no risk shows nothing. The ballots view groups questions by risk class, with the approval rule beside each group, so you see why they can't approve themselves.

8Titles, Grammar and Tone

"Titles, grammar and tone should be defined, and fully rewritten for NightHall for all items."

What makes NightHall titles hard to read

  • Metaphor titles hide the subject: "A Saturday Night at Risk", "Every Stranger Waits", "Keep the Door True", "Learn from the Night", "Freedom With Proofs", "Close What Time Ended". LiteSpec's own authoring rule already warns that "a metaphor reads smoothly while hiding what the project means".
  • One type, three grammars. Problems mix noun phrases ("Hidden Ticket Fees"), clauses ("Costs Rise, Demand Turns Late") and fragments ("Proof Before Commitment").
  • Mixed casing. Requirements and some reactions use sentence case ("Pay as you go fee", "Record lead on sandbox started"), while pages use Title Case.
  • No title names who. None of the 30 problem titles names the affected actor.
  • Codes and jargon without explanation: "M1 Five Signed Partners", "V1 Does Not Fit the Calendar", "Refund Rail Windows", "Eenmanszaak with Triggers".
  • One-word features say nothing: "Audience", "Event Day", "Event Money".
  • British spelling in records ("Favours", "colour"), although LiteSpec sets American spelling for records. NightHall's en-GB rule is for UI strings.

One title form per record type

TypeFormNowRewritten
ProblemClause: who, then the pain, present tenseHidden Ticket FeesOrganizers Cannot See the Whole Ticket Bill
FeatureNoun phrase naming the capabilityEvent DayDoor Operation with Offline Scanning
GoalOutcome noun phrase; number and date stay in fieldsM1 Five Signed PartnersFive Signed Design Partners
JourneyVerb plus object: the traveler's taskKeep the Door TrueReconcile Seats, Guests, and Conflicts at the Door
ActorRole noun phraseReport Recipientkept
RequirementNoun phrase naming the assertion, Title CasePay as you go feePay-as-You-Go Ticket Fee
ConstraintSubject noun phrase; authority in its fieldRefund Rail WindowsRefund Windows per Payment Method
DecisionThe chosen outcome as a noun phrasePermission Records Are the One Access ListOne Access List from Permission Records
ResearchThe question it answersWho Else Sells Dutch Tickets, and What They Chargekept
Use case, job, runbookVerb firstNotify Buyers of Event Change (job runs send-event-change-notices)Send Event Change Notices
RuleAssertion as a clauseGross never counts as NightHall incomeGross Sales Never Count as NightHall Income
ScreenThe place name the user seesAudience Automations Enable After EventAutomation Timing After Events

Prose and tone

  • Statements: present tense, active voice, third person, one sentence, no modal words. LiteSpec already requires this and NightHall breaks it ("The shop must match the poster...").
  • Sentences of 25 words at most in records. NightHall's checklist already sets this for UI copy.
  • A situation or explanation restates who and what's at stake in its first lines, for the reader who arrives cold. A pointer may follow the evidence, never replace it.
  • Tone: the business explaining itself to its founder. Plain words, checkable facts, honest roles; no selling and no decoration. This is NightHall's existing six-attribute voice, carried from UI copy into records.
Recommendation

Keep Title Case everywhere: 90 percent of titles already use it, and one rule is the only rule a check can enforce. Put the title forms and prose rules in LiteSpec's record language page, with checks for length, final period, modal words and casing. Keep voice, banned metaphors and spelling for UI in NightHall's writing records. Run the NightHall rewrite after the record changes in sections 1 to 7 land, so each record is rewritten once.

The worker produced 44 sample rewrites. I corrected some before using them here: one "after" title still contained a modal ("Must Not"), and some added dates that sit in prose pages rather than in goal fields.

9Completion over Approval

"What matters most to me is the state of completion of the overall feature and requirement, rather than approved, draft or whatnot."

What the model computes today

LiteSpec already computes completion words at the bottom of the tree: implemented (code found for a use case, rule, event or state), verified (every scenario of a use case has a passing, fresh proof), met (every fulfiller of a requirement is verified and its measure passes), tested, and exercised (for a journey step). Nothing is computed for features, journeys as a whole, topics, goals or problems. The only state a feature has is the hand-written lifecycle.

NightHall, traced end to end

FactValueMeaning
Use cases with code1,281 of 1,286Substantially built
Use cases verified0No test run in the model, so unknown rather than failed
Requirements met0 of 942Same cause
Features by lifecycle39 / 71 / 1 / 0planned / refused / later / shipped
feature/sell-tickets37 requirementsApproved, "planned for v1"; checkout handler, endpoint and screens all present
requirement/buyers.no-card-surcharge0 fulfillersApproved and cited by the primary journey, but nothing in Behavior keeps it. Its finding is parked in a gap exception, so the book shows the same "Not yet met" as a requirement with 18 working fulfillers.

So the book can't currently tell apart four very different states: nothing written, written but not built, built but proof unknown, and proven. And shipped, the one word that looks like completion, has never been written once.

Three designs

DesignHeadlineRisk of a false 100%Scanning 55 features
A. Stage ladder. Each record gets one computed stage (unfulfilled, specified, implemented, proven), and a parent is only as far as its weakest in-scope childOne word, plus the child holding it backLow: it names what holds itSortable, comparable
B. Percentages. Averages of childrenA percentageHigh: park the hard requirements and the rest reads 100%Sortable but misleading
C. Checklist only. One row per required link: present, missing, not due, or unknownNoneNoneYou have to open every page
Recommendation

Use Design A as the headline, with Design C's checklist as the evidence underneath and counts ("12 of 37") only inside the checklist. Keep approval: it's an accountable human decision and still gates release. Put completion first on the page and move Status below it. Treat "proof unknown, no test run" as its own state; never show it as failure. Make shipped honest with an advisory check that flags a feature marked shipped while an in-scope requirement is below proven.

Prerequisite: NightHall needs a test run and docs/proof/proofs.json in its model build. Without them, every feature will correctly but uselessly read "Implemented, proof unknown".

10A Page That Stands Alone

"Most items don't have enough context when reading and reviewing them in the book. I might open an item out of nowhere without reading the full tree." "There should be a small icon allowing copying the title and the id."

Why a cold page fails

The book's tree placement is sound; the problem is in the detail renderer. It makes five moves on every page, all confirmed in book.js:

  1. It hides the type. The label is rendered hidden, and "What is a problem?" sits in a collapsed details element.
  2. It drops the id. It's only in the URL hash and the file path.
  3. It moves links to the rail. affects, serves, solves and advances are suppressed on the page and shown only in the right rail, so who and what-it-connects-to leave the reading column.
  4. It encodes facts as badges. A feature's lifecycle goes into a coloured pill, and a regex (factKey()) then guesses which field the pill was.
  5. It answers "approved?" when you asked "how complete?".

One page anatomy for every record type

BlockContents
1. HeaderBreadcrumb as the parent chain; title; always-visible type line "Problem: Which pain does someone have today?"; identity line with the id in mono, source file and line, and Copy title and Copy ID icon buttons
2. LeadThe record's own one-sentence answer: statement, summary, offering, or the new journey description
3. CompletionThe computed stage and what holds it back (section 9)
4. FieldsOne aligned two-column table: who (affects, actor), place (solves, advances, serves), status and approval, risk class, lifecycle, plus type fields. Labels come from LiteSpec terms. No pills.
5. ProseProse fields in schema order, then explanation sections under their headings
6. LinksOutgoing and incoming links, grouped by relation ("Solved by", "Cited by"), each with its statement, expandable instead of cut at 220 characters
7. RailOnly the goal-to-behavior trace, implementation and proof
Recommendation

Build this as one generic renderer with small per-type content plug-ins (journey steps, aggregate states, the screen image, scenario tables), instead of adding the blocks to each of the roughly 30 per-type renderers. One shape per kind, by construction. Add a book test that fails on a hidden type line, a badge holding a fact, or a missing id line, so the shape can't drift back. The copy buttons need about 20 lines in header() plus a clipboard fallback for pages opened as files.

Practice agrees. GitHub puts the issue number in the title line, Redoc makes every operation deep-linkable from a static host, and Nielsen Norman Group says breadcrumbs should mirror the true hierarchy. The anatomy above is the common shape of Backstage, GitHub, Linear and DOORS Next item pages.

11Fields Instead of Badges

"Badges and beautiful elements and card in card don't cut it for the book UI; it should follow consistency and explicit fields with alignment, like each page's fields."

Design systems agree with you. Atlassian says "use badge for numbers, lozenge to highlight an item's status, tag to categorize". GOV.UK says to use adjectives, not verbs, for tag names, and to start with the smallest number of statuses. For facts about an item, GOV.UK's summary list (key, value, action, one row per fact) is the direct precedent. Nielsen Norman Group describes cards as entry points to a destination, not property sheets.

The book audit found about 18 decorative elements. The main ones:

Element nowEncodesShould become
Coloured badge() pillsLifecycle, kind, scope, directionA labelled row in the field table
"T1" tier tagRiskField "Risk: Money, approved by a named person"
Proof chips (implemented, no scenarios)Proof stateThe Completion block and a Proof column
Initials avatars on journey stepsStep actorText "Actor: Team Member" (initials fail for systems)
Tiles inside sectionsMeasure, access, scheduleRows in the one field table
Result, option and effect cardsOutcomes, pros and cons, effectsAligned tables, so values line up down the page
Five callout box stylesFinished when, authority, examplesPlain sections under a field-label heading
Three generations of CSS card and border overridesNoneDeleted: the cascade is why card-in-card survived
Recommendation

Every fact on a record page becomes a labelled, aligned row. Keep pills only for controls (filters) and status icons in the dense navigation list, where a legend explains them. Question cards stay cards because they're actions, but each gets an aligned header row.

12Long Lists

"It's hard to read long lists of items; grouping by topic matters, and maybe it should be applied to all layers."

NightHall's book holds 21,919 records: 386 screens, 942 requirements, 1,286 use cases and 7,541 results. Inside a parent, the outline groups only by type. The list view caps at 400 rows and groups only by type, layer, status, decider or tier. Detail pages truncate silently: 150 children, 8 rail links per label, 6 scenarios.

ListGroup byField it uses
RequirementsTopicAlready the parent
Use cases, rules, reactions, jobsModule, then aggregateIdentifier home, aggregate
ScreensEntry point, then floorplanentryPoint, floorplan
JourneysLead actor, then goalactor, serves
ProblemsPrimary affected actor, then goalaffects, via solving features
FeaturesLifecycle, then completion stagelifecycle; 71 of 111 are refused, so collapse those by default
ActorsKindkind
Recommendation

Use these groupings everywhere: in the list view first, then as a second level in the outline. Group headers stay visible and show counts with completion ("Webshop: 24 screens, 18 implemented"). Each row shows type, title, status in words and the first line of its statement, so you can tell what a row is before opening it. Replace silent truncation with "Show all N". All of these are computed from existing fields, so nothing is invented.

13Screenshots on Screen Pages

"Screenshots of screens in the book; the screenshot should be the focus of a screen's page."

The book has no image anywhere today. The good news: NightHall already photographs every route. Its admin and webshop Playwright configs have a gallery project that captures every route in light and dark at 1440 and 390 pixels, to test-results/gallery/<route>--<theme>--<width>.png, "a review tool, never a gate" (apps/admin/tests/gallery/gallery.spec.ts). The model already maps each screen to its route file. The join key exists on both sides.

OptionProsCons
A. A screenshot path field on each screen recordExplicitHand-maintained and goes stale; 386 paths to keep right
B. The book derives the file name from the routeNo authoringTies the book to NightHall's file-name convention
C. The model builder records each screen's capture (path and capture date) from a configured gallery folderThe fact enters LiteSpec first, as the book rules require. Staleness becomes data ("captured 12 days before this build").The builder must know where the gallery lives (one config entry)
Recommendation

Option C. On a screen page the image comes right after the title, at full column width, captioned with route, theme, width and capture date, with a switch for phone and dark. With no capture, the page says plainly whether the route exists but wasn't captured, or no page carries the screen yet. Copy one desktop light PNG per screen into the book, and load the others on demand.

14Business and Operations in LiteSpec

"I see so many things in LiteSpec about how we operate the business, versioning, deployment and so on."

You're right, and it's by design

LiteSpec says so itself. docs/core/intent.md:28: "Product intent is what the business commits to: what it sells, to whom, at what price, and in which markets, plus how the company runs and what comes next." The area example lists business/pricing.yaml, company/legal-and-tax.yaml and roadmap/milestones.yaml. docs/core/system.md:13 explains where this came from: one person operates the company that wrote LiteSpec, so product, engineering and company operation were one job, and the standard turned that one company's way of working into every consumer's contract.

The Wonder worker sorted every page by one test: who can tell whether it holds?

ClassTestExamples
(a) Specifies the applicationA user or an automated test can tellUse cases, rules, screens, tenancy, jobs, outbox, most extensions
(b) Engineering practiceOnly someone with repository or cloud access can tellcore/release (45 provisions), quality/ci (18), quality/operations (29), workspace/* (48), containers, stage
(c) Running the companyOnly the founder's bank account, diary or contracts can tellBusiness, company, go-to-market, markets and roadmap topics; company goals; founder-risk problems; business procedures written as runbooks
(d) LiteSpec's own upkeepOnly a LiteSpec maintainer can tellcore/maintaining, half of authoring, provision index

In NightHall, (c) is 30 topic pages (business 6, company 6, go-to-market 7, markets 4, roadmap 4, customers 3), most of the 8 goals (run rate, churn, partner counts), about 10 problems, and business procedures among the 46 runbooks (for example programme-over-budget, counsel-tcs-swap). None of the comparable standards puts (c) inside the specification: arc42, C4, ISO 29148, IEEE 1016, OpenAPI, AsyncAPI, Twelve-Factor, Backstage, Spec Kit and Kiro all leave it out. Twelve-Factor covers the running app and says nothing about prices or launch dates. Spec Kit and Kiro make the feature the unit.

OptionWhat movesProsCons
1. Keep everythingNothingOne place for everything; no migrationThe book can't show the product without the company; every consumer carries a regime sized for one company
2. Move (b) and (c) into opt-in extensionsA Delivery extension for release, CI and operations, and a Company extension for business topicsUses the extension mechanism LiteSpec already trusts; NightHall keeps everything by selecting bothCompany facts still mix into problem and goal traceability unless the extension fences them
3. Take (c) out; move (b)'s heavy half into a Delivery extensionCompany facts go to a company handbook (plain documents) and come back in only as a constraint or research when they bind the productThe smallest honest core; the book becomes a product book you can review end to end; matches every comparable standardYou lose seeing everything in one place; LiteSpec loses its "whole company system" identity
Recommendation

Option 3, with one rule that holds the boundary: an Intent or Behavior record states only behavior the application performs, data it holds, or a limit it enforces. A person's time, a price as an offer, a market entry, a hiring or sales action, or a launch date enters only as a constraint or as dated research. Checks: a problem must name a non-staff actor; a goal must be movable by a journey or quality requirement; intent area folders named business, company, go-to-market, markets or roadmap are rejected; a runbook must be named by an alert, job, reaction or failure policy.

Prices need care. Plan entitlements the software enforces stay as application behavior (settings and permissions), while the price list as a company offer leaves.

If you want to keep LiteSpec as a whole-company system, take Option 2 instead. In that case the book must show the Company chapters in their own group, so reviewing the product comes first. Either way, don't keep Option 1 unchanged.

Order of Work

The order matters: each step changes what the next one writes, so nothing is rewritten twice.

StepWorkRepositoryUnblocks
1Decide the five open decisions belowYouEverything
2Standard changes: problem admission rule and fields; actors limited to person and organization; journey description; risk class plus approval table; title forms and prose rules; scope boundary rule and Delivery extensionLiteSpec3, 4
3Model builder: completion stages, screenshot capture facts, glossary-term checkLiteSpec4
4Book: generic page anatomy, copy controls, fields not badges, groupings, completion block, screen image, book hygiene testBookReview
5NightHall migration: re-home 17 problems, deepen 13; remove 16 actors; write 114 journey descriptions and split the 21-step journey; define design partner; move company material out; load a test run and proof ledger into the modelNightHall6
6NightHall rewrite of every title and statement to the new forms, by an agent swarm with a pattern briefNightHallDone

Steps 2 to 4 belong in one LiteSpec release. Steps 5 and 6 are large but mechanical once the shapes exist: most of the work is agent writing that you approve in batches.

Decisions for You

#DecisionOptionsMy recommendation
1Is LiteSpec a product specification or a whole-company system?Option 3 (company out) or Option 2 (company as an extension)Option 3. This is an identity choice for LiteSpec, not a tidy-up, so it's yours.
2What does "shipped" mean?Drop it from completion; compute it from a release register; or keep it hand-written with a check against proofKeep it hand-written with the check now; compute it once a release register exists
3Where does the organizer sit among actors?Keep as an organization actor, or move to a new customer typeKeep as an organization actor: it's who has the problems
4Merge a-saturday-night-at-risk into organizers-doubt-a-new-supplier?Merge, or keep the first-night decision distinctMerge
5Title casingTitle Case everywhere, or sentence case everywhereTitle Case: 90 percent already, and it's checkable

Method and Evidence

Eight Muse Code workers ran read-only in the two repositories, each briefed with your feedback verbatim, the LiteSpec principles and its own question. I read every report, checked its load-bearing claims against the repository or the source page, and corrected what didn't hold. The worker reports are kept in .agents/delegate/book-review-2026-11-02-1842/done/ in the LiteSpec repository.
